extracted.intended_audience: first-time inventors and entrepreneurs drafting their first U.S. patent application
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, tactical guidance for inventors preparing their first U.S. patent filing (provisional or non‑provisional), focused on claim drafting, disclosure strategy, figures, embodiments, and prior art searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the claims, then work backwards
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claim 1 first, decide which elements are truly essential, then write the specification to support every word in that claim. If a term appears in a claim but is not anchored in the spec, you have a 112(b) problem waiting to happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claims define what you actually own — structure the entire application around them. Identify essential claim elements before drafting the spec and ensure each claim term is expressly supported in the specification to avoid written‑description/claim‑support issues (the author cites a potential 112(b) problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Your independent claim is probably too narrow
rubrics_metrics.description: First-timers reflexively describe their commercial product, producing claims with many non‑load‑bearing elements. Strip each independent claim down to the minimum combination that distinguishes over the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit each claim limitation and remove anything unnecessary (e.g., 'wherein the user clicks a button' is likely an unnecessary limitation). Focus independent claims on the minimal distinguishing features versus closest prior art to preserve breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent claims of different scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not file with just one independent claim. File three or four: one broad, one of moderate scope, and one narrow but commercially aligned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim diversity is a prosecution/post‑grant hedge: if the broad claim is killed, narrower claims may survive. Structure claim sets to include varied scopes (broad, medium, narrow) tailored to both legal strength and commercial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe three embodiments, not one
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if you only built one prototype, describe (a) the prototype, (b) a more general version with components swapped for functional equivalents, and (c) a degenerate or simplified version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing multiple embodiments makes later claim breadth and claim construction easier. Include functional equivalents and simplified/degenerate examples to guard against overly narrow interpretations and to support claim amendments or continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'Patent Profanity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'essential,' 'critical,' 'must,' 'always,' 'the invention is,' and 'the present invention requires' are landmines. Courts read these as disclaimers of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer non‑absolute phrasing such as 'in some embodiments,' 'may include,' or 'one example.' Avoid absolute terms that can be construed as limiting or disclaiming claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw the figures yourself first
rubrics_metrics.description: You will discover gaps in your own understanding when you try to label every reference number. Aim for one figure per concept. Block diagrams beat photographs for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketching figures forces precision about structures and relationships; use clear block diagrams rather than photos when possible. Ensure each figure supports the described embodiments and claim elements with reference numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose more than you want to claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure is cheap; you cannot add new matter later. If you have alternative materials, alternative orderings, alternative ranges — put them in the spec even if you do not currently claim them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alternatives, variations, and ranges in the specification to preserve options for continuations and claim amendments. Over‑disclose to create 'fodder for continuations' and to avoid losing rights later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional applications are not a free pass
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional only gets you a priority date for what is actually disclosed. A two‑page sketch labeled 'provisional' gives you a priority date for two pages of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a thin provisional to protect un‑disclosed subject matter — if your non‑provisional claims things not present in the provisional, you lose priority for those claims. Prepare sufficiently detailed provisionals if you intend to claim priority to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get a real search done before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a Google search. A real prior art search by a professional searcher costs $500–$2,000 and routinely surfaces the closest art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in a professional prior art search before drafting to identify the closest references and shape claim strategy appropriately. Knowing the closest art up front can save years of wasted prosecution on claims that read on older references.
